articleBody:
- [ ] Property boundary survey — Confirms your exact legal lot lines so your new bedroom suite does not violate local zoning setbacks or maximum lot-coverage caps.
- [ ] Existing home foundation assessment — Ensures your current foundation and soil conditions can tie into a new slab or support second-story framing loads.
- [ ] HOA architectural guidelines and approvals — Prevents costly redesigns by establishing approved exterior finish materials, window styles, and roofline profiles beforehand.
- [ ] Bedroom egress window specifications — Confirms planned windows meet building code requirements for emergency escape openings, minimum glass area, and sill heights.
- [ ] Bathroom fixture clearance diagram — Verifies required spacing in front of and between the vanity, toilet, and walk-in shower for daily comfort and local code compliance.
- [ ] HVAC load calculation — Checks whether your current air conditioning unit can condition the added square footage or if a dedicated heat pump zone is necessary.
- [ ] Electrical panel capacity check — Ensures your main service panel has available breaker space for added lighting circuits, bathroom heaters, and modern bedroom outlets.
- [ ] Plumbing sewer tie-in plan — Determines the slope, drain venting, and tie-in route to your main sewer pipe before foundation work commences.
- [ ] Temporary living arrangements plan — Establishes how your household will manage noise, dust, and potential utility shutoffs while active construction takes place.

How to use this checklist:
Work through these items sequentially during your early planning phase before finalizing architectural drawings or ordering materials. Addressing zoning, structural tie-ins, and mechanical capacity early protects your budget from sudden change orders. 

What to Do Next:
Because primary suite additions impact foundations, framing, rooflines, and mechanical systems, working with an experienced licensed contractor ensures drawings, permits, and inspections stay properly aligned.
